name: Dolomites Alta Via 1
summary: A roughly 125 km north–south traverse of the eastern Dolomites from Lago di Braies to Belluno, staying in rifugi throughout. The most walked of the Alte Vie: waymarked paths with no obligatory via ferrata, though a few sections are cabled.

name: Dolomites Alta Via 2
summary: About 180 km from Bressanone/Brixen south to Croce d'Aune near Feltre, crossing the Puez-Odle, Sella, Marmolada and Pale di San Martino groups with some 11,000 m of ascent. Several stages are protected via ferrata, and a harness and lanyard are normally carried.

name: Dolomites Alta Via 3
summary: The "via dei camosci", about 100–120 km from Villabassa to Longarone by way of the Tre Cime, Cadini, Sorapiss and Marmarole. Graded EE: exposed and cabled in places, with long, lightly travelled stages.

name: Dolomites Alta Via 4
summary: The Grohmann route, roughly 85 km from San Candido to Pieve di Cadore through the Sesto Dolomites, the Cadini di Misurina and the Sorapiss. Short by Alta Via standards but technically the most demanding of the first four, with equipped and via ferrata sections.

name: Dolomites Alta Via 5
summary: The Alta Via di Tiziano, about 90 km from Sesto to Pieve di Cadore across the Popera and Croda dei Toni groups, the Marmarole and the flank of the Antelao. The Marmarole section is remote, cabled and often in cloud, and is described by its guardians as bordering on mountaineering.

name: Dolomites Alta Via 6
summary: The Alta Via dei Silenzi, some 180 km in eleven stages from Sappada to Vittorio Veneto through the Friulian and eastern Dolomites. Its difficulty is less technical than logistical: several nights are in unstaffed bivouacs and long stretches carry almost no other walkers.
